title: A global lending channel unplugged? Does U.S. monetary policy affect cross-border and affiliate lending by global U.S. banks?
abstract: We examine how U.S. monetary policy affects the international activities of U.S. banks. We access a rarely studied U.S. bank-level regulatory dataset to assess at a quarterly frequency how changes in the U.S. Federal funds rate (before the crisis) and quantitative easing (after the onset of the crisis) affect changes in cross-border claims by U.S. banks across countries, maturities and sectors, and also affect changes in claims by their foreign affiliates. We find robust evidence consistent with the existence of a potent global bank lending channel. In response to changes in U.S. monetary conditions, U.S. banks strongly adjust their cross-border claims in both the pre- and post-crisis period. However, we also find that U.S. bank affiliate claims respond mainly to host country monetary conditions.
summary_en: Does US monetary policy spread internationally through US banks' foreign activities? Temesváry, Ongena and Owen access a quarterly US bank regulatory dataset to test whether changes in the Fed funds rate (pre-crisis) and quantitative-easing operations (post-crisis) affect US banks' cross-border claims and the activities of their foreign affiliates. They find robust evidence of a global bank lending channel: US banks adjust their cross-border claims in response to US monetary policy in both pre- and post-crisis periods. Foreign affiliates of US banks, however, respond mainly to host-country monetary conditions, not US ones — they 'localise' their behaviour.
data_used: US Federal Reserve quarterly bank-level regulatory dataset (FR 2502, Y-9C, FFIEC 002) on cross-border claims and foreign-affiliate activities, 1980s-2010s.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for IMF, BIS and central banks (including MNB) that US monetary policy transmits via US banks' cross-border lending — a globally important channel that affects emerging-market financing conditions. Relevant for MNB macroprudential monitoring of Hungarian companies' USD-denominated borrowing exposure.
